parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A man phones a house-sitting agency to arrange for someone to look after his home and pets while he is on holiday.
script: Good morning, Homewatch House-Sitting, Tessa speaking. How can I help?
Morning. I'm hoping to arrange a house-sitter for when we're away on holiday. A friend of mine used your service last year and she couldn't recommend it highly enough.
That's lovely to hear. I'll take a few details first, and then we can talk about exactly what you need. Could I have your surname, please?
Could you spell that for me?
Thank you, Mr Brannigan. And what's the best number to reach you on?
My mobile is the easiest. It's 07845 336 192. I don't really answer the landline during the day.
07845 336 192. Got that. And the address of the house?
It's 28 Fenwick Road, in Marlow Heath. Fenwick is F-E-N-W-I-C-K.
Lovely, thank you. Now, when are you going away?
We fly out on the 9th of August and we're back on the 23rd. Actually, I should say that I originally booked the 8th, but the airline changed our flight, so it's definitely the 9th now.
Right, so the sitter would need to be with you from the 9th. That's two weeks. Now, can you tell me about the animals? Our sitters always like to know exactly what they're taking on.

Well, we've got a dog, an old spaniel called Hector, who's no trouble at all, and two cats. Well, three cats now, to be honest. We took in a rescue kitten last month, a little tabby, so I'd better count her.
Three cats and a dog. That's fine. Is there anything the sitter should know about their care? Any medication, for example?

Yes, the older cat, Biscuit, has to have a tablet with his breakfast every morning. The vet did suggest injections at one point, but that was far too complicated, so it's a tablet hidden in his food. He doesn't make a fuss about it.

That's no problem at all. Our sitters are used to that sort of thing. Now, let me explain the two packages we offer. The Standard package is 28 pounds a night, and the sitter stays in your house, feeds and walks the animals and keeps an eye on everything. The Premium package is 35 pounds a night, and that includes some cleaning and laundry as well.
I don't think we need the cleaning. We'll leave the house tidy. The Standard one sounds right, so 28 pounds a night.
Perfect. With Standard, the sitter will also water your plants and bring in anything delivered. Would you like them to collect the newspaper from the doorstep as well?
Oh, I'm cancelling the newspaper while we're away. But yes, if they could bring the post in every day, that would be great. It always piles up on the mat and then it looks as if nobody's home.
Of course. Now, we always ask for the name of someone nearby who can be contacted in an emergency, in case the sitter has a problem and can't reach you.
That would be our neighbour, Mrs Okonkwo, at number 30. She has a spare key as well. Let me spell it for you, because people never get it right. O-K-O-N-K-W-O.
Thank you. Now, our manager likes the sitter to meet the owners and the animals before the holiday begins, so that everyone's comfortable. Would Monday evening suit you?
Monday's difficult, I'm afraid. I tend to work late on Mondays. How about Thursday, the week before we leave? Around six o'clock would be ideal.
Thursday at six should be fine. I'll check which sitter is free and I'll email you to confirm. Is there anything else you'd like to ask?
Just one thing. Does the sitter have to be police-checked? I'd feel better knowing.
Absolutely. All our sitters are checked and insured, and we can send you a profile with a photo before they arrive.
That's reassuring. Thank you very much for your help.
My pleasure, Mr Brannigan. You'll hear from me by the end of the week. Enjoy your holiday.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: A volunteer gives a talk to visitors at an open evening of a neighbourhood tool-lending library.
script: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming along to the open evening at the Northfield Tool Library. My name's Greg, and I'm one of the volunteers. I'm going to spend the next few minutes explaining how the library works, and then you're very welcome to wander around and have a look at the shelves.

Let me start with how it all began. People often assume the council set the library up as part of a waste reduction campaign, and I can see why, because it does fit in well with that. Others think the founders copied a scheme they'd seen overseas. In fact, neither is true. It started four years ago, when the old hardware shop on Mill Street closed down. The owner, Mr Pryce, was retiring, and rather than sell off his stock cheaply, he gave the whole lot to a group of neighbours who'd been talking about sharing tools. That gave us about two hundred drills, saws and spanners to begin with.

At first we operated out of a shipping container behind the library, which was freezing in winter and boiling in summer. We were then offered a room in the community centre, but it was only available at weekends, so that didn't work for long. Eventually the church let us have its old hall, which is where we are tonight. It's a big, dry space, and we've even got a proper workshop corner, which I'll show you in a moment.

Now, a few numbers. When we opened, we hoped to get about 400 members in the first year, and we managed that within six months, which was a lovely surprise. Today we have just over 900 members, and we're really proud of that. The collection has grown too. We now have more than 1,400 tools, from basic hammers to a rather fierce-looking tile cutter.

So, how do you join? It's very simple. When we started, we asked for a deposit from every new member, but we found it put people off, so we stopped doing that. And you don't have to attend an induction session just to borrow a screwdriver, either. What we do ask is that everyone shows us a utility bill or something similar when they sign up, so that we know you live in the neighbourhood. That keeps the library a local resource, and it's the only thing we insist on.

People sometimes ask what our biggest challenge is. Well, it isn't space any more, now that we're in the hall, and it isn't late returns either, because most members are very good about bringing things back on time. The real difficulty is finding enough volunteers. We need people to staff the desk, to check and sharpen the tools, and to help members choose the right equipment. If any of you have a few spare hours a month, please talk to me afterwards.

Now, a word about the rules, because some items are treated differently from others. Take the pressure washer. It used to be available for a week, but it's so popular in spring that we had to change it, and now you can only borrow it for one day. Then there's the tile cutter I mentioned. That's an expensive piece of kit, so for that one we do take a deposit of 20 pounds, which you get back when you return it undamaged.

The chainsaw is another special case. We're not being fussy, it's simply a question of safety, so you can't just turn up and take it away. You have to complete a short training session with one of our experienced volunteers first, and then it's yours to borrow. We run those sessions on the first Saturday of every month.

Then there's the wallpaper steamer. Everyone seems to decide to redecorate at the same time, so it needs to be reserved at least a week in advance. You can do that online or at the desk. And finally, for ordinary hand tools, such as hammers, saws and spanners, there are no special conditions at all. You can borrow them for up to two weeks, free of charge, and if you need them for longer, just ask.
I think that's everything from me. If you have any questions, please grab me or any of the people wearing green aprons. Thanks again for coming, and enjoy looking around.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two students and their tutor discuss a literature review on teenagers and screen time.
script: Come in, both of you, and take a seat. Right, I've read your draft literature review on teenagers and screen time. Before I say anything about it, remind me how you came to choose this topic.
It was mostly Anika's idea. I think she was inspired by that documentary everyone was talking about.

Actually, no. I only saw that later. It started with my little sister. She went through a phase of being on her tablet every evening, and her mood changed completely. I wanted to find out whether that was typical or whether I was imagining it.

Well, personal curiosity is a perfectly good starting point, as long as it doesn't bias you. Now, to the draft itself. I'll be honest, it's thorough, and I can see you've read widely. My main criticism is that it reads like a list. You summarise one study after another, but you hardly ever say whether a study is any good.
We were worried about the word limit, so we kept each summary short.
The length isn't the problem, and neither is the structure, which is clear enough. What's missing is evaluation. A literature review should weigh the evidence, not just report it.
Right. So we need to be more critical about the methods the researchers used.
Exactly. Now, what about the time period you're covering?
We started with everything from 2000 onwards, but a lot of the early research is really about television, not screens in the modern sense.
So we'd like to restrict it to studies carried out since smartphones became common, which was around 2010.
I'd agree with that. I wouldn't go as far as limiting it to the last five years, though. You'd miss some useful work. Is there anything you're stuck on?

Yes, there's one real headache. Nobody defines screen time in the same way. Some studies count only recreational use, others include homework, and some just ask about phones. That makes it hard to group the studies by theme, which is what we planned to do.
That's actually a finding in its own right, so say so in the review. Now, one more thing about the shape of the whole piece. How do you plan to finish?
We thought we'd end with some advice for parents about how much screen time is safe.
I'd steer clear of that. It goes beyond what a review can support. Better to finish by pointing out where the research is weakest and what future studies should investigate.
That makes sense. We'll do that instead.
Good. Let's go through some of your main sources, then, so I can show you what I mean by evaluation. Where would you like to start?
With Aldous, the 2014 study. It's cited everywhere, but it relied entirely on teenagers filling in diaries about their own use, and I suspect they simply guessed.
Yes, self-reporting is notoriously unreliable. You should say that in your text. What about the next one?
Tanaka and Brooks is much stronger, I think. They followed the same group of students for six years, so you can actually see how habits changed over time.
Indeed. That's a real strength, and it deserves more space in your review than it has at the moment.
The Fernandez report is more awkward. It found no harm at all from heavy use, which is interesting, but it was paid for by a video games company.
Then you must flag that. Readers will want to know who paid for the research.
And the Ng survey only involved forty-two families, so we can't really generalise from it, however interesting the results are.
Quite. That's a limitation worth mentioning. And the last one on your list?
The Eriksson review. It's very well put together, but it only covered children under ten, so it doesn't really tell us about teenagers.
A fair point. Include it, but be clear about that limit. Right, I think you know what to do. Shall we say another draft in two weeks?
That's fine. Thank you very much.
Thanks, Dr Hollis. That was really helpful.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecturer gives a talk on the history of spectacles.
script: Good afternoon, everyone. In today's lecture I'd like to look at something most of us take completely for granted, which is the humble pair of spectacles. It is easy to forget that for most of human history, anyone whose eyesight began to fail simply had to put up with it. Today I want to trace how that changed.

Let us begin before spectacles existed. Scholars, and particularly monks who spent their lives copying manuscripts, often found their eyesight failing in middle age. From around the eleventh century, some of them used what were known as reading stones. These were simple lumps of polished quartz or glass, shaped like half a ball, which were placed on top of the page to magnify the letters. Quartz was the usual material in the early days, since good clear glass was expensive and difficult to make. They worked rather well, but of course you had to hold one in your hand, which made writing impossible.

The decisive step came towards the end of the thirteenth century. We cannot be certain who deserves the credit, but the evidence points to northern Italy, where glassmakers had developed some skill in making clear glass. A sermon preached around the year 1300 refers to spectacles as an invention less than twenty years old. People sometimes assume that France or Germany was the birthplace, but the earliest records are all Italian, and I am fairly confident that this is where the idea began.

These early spectacles were very different from what we wear today. They consisted of two magnifying lenses, each set in a frame, and the two frames were riveted together at the handles. The frames themselves were made of horn, although you will sometimes read that they were made of metal. Metal was used later on, but the first frames were horn, or sometimes wood or leather in cheaper versions. There were no arms to hook over the ears. The wearer either held the spectacles up to the eyes, or pinched them on to the bridge of the nose, where they had a tendency to slip off. You can imagine that nobody wore them while running for a bus.

All of these early lenses were convex, which means they were thicker in the middle. They helped people who found it hard to see things close up, which is the usual problem in middle age. They did nothing for people who were short-sighted, who struggled to see things in the distance. For that you needed concave lenses, which are thinner in the middle, and these took a long time to appear. A famous portrait painted in the early sixteenth century shows Pope Leo the Tenth holding a concave lens up to his eye, and this is one of the earliest pieces of evidence we have that short sight was being treated at all.

The next challenge was keeping spectacles on the face. In the sixteenth century, makers in Spain experimented with silk ribbons, which were attached to the frames and looped over the wearer's ears. It was an improvement, but not a perfect one, and the ribbons wore out quickly. Other solutions were tried over the following centuries, including weights and even strings tied behind the head. It was not until 1727 that an optician in London, Edward Scarlett, made the next major advance. He added rigid arms, known as temples, which rested on the ears. That is, in essence, the design we still use today.

Now, you might think that once the design was settled, everyone could simply buy a pair. In fact, spectacles remained a luxury for a very long time. A pair cost a skilled worker several weeks' wages, and many people simply could not afford them. It was only in the nineteenth century, with the arrival of mass production, that spectacles became affordable to ordinary people. Factories could turn out frames and lenses in large numbers, and prices fell dramatically. Opticians' shops appeared on high streets, and eye tests began to be offered for the first time.

The twentieth century brought further changes in materials. Glass lenses had always been heavy and could shatter, so from the 1950s plastic lenses became increasingly popular. They were much lighter and safer, and today most lenses are plastic. Frames, too, changed, and became fashion items, with people owning several pairs. Modern lenses are also treated with special coatings, which reduce glare from screens and headlights and help to keep scratches off the surface.

To sum up, then, the story of spectacles is really one of gradual improvement over seven centuries, with advances in glassmaking, materials and manufacturing each making a difference. In next week's session, we will move on to the history of the microscope, which grew out of exactly the same lens-making skills. Thank you.

passages.title: The Story of Rubber
paras: A  The earliest known use of rubber is far older than most people imagine. Some three thousand years ago, the peoples of Central America were collecting the milky white latex that oozes from certain trees when the bark is cut. They mixed it with the juice of a local vine and produced a material that could be moulded into balls for a ceremonial game, into waterproof containers and into figures offered to the gods. When the Spanish arrived in the sixteenth century, they were astonished by the balls, which bounced far higher than anything stuffed with hair or wool. Yet they found little other use for the substance, and for two hundred years it remained a curiosity.

B  Even its name arrived late. In 1770 the English chemist Joseph Priestley noticed that a lump of the material removed pencil marks, and shops began to sell small cubes as 'rubbers'. Europeans soon tried to turn it into something more useful, but with little success, because raw rubber has a serious flaw: in cold weather it becomes hard and brittle, and in heat it turns soft and sticky. In 1823 the Scottish chemist Charles Macintosh sandwiched a layer of rubber between two pieces of cloth to make waterproof coats. They were an immediate novelty, but they smelled unpleasant, and in the summer the fabric dissolved into a gummy mess. Customers returned them in large numbers, and the early rubber companies went out of business.

C  The problem was finally solved by Charles Goodyear, an American inventor who spent years in poverty and debt, experimenting with rubber in kitchens and workshops. According to his own account, in 1839 he accidentally dropped a mixture of rubber and sulphur on to a hot stove and found that it charred at the edges but remained firm and flexible. Careful experiments showed that heating rubber with sulphur changed it permanently, so that it stayed elastic across a wide range of temperatures. The process was later named vulcanisation, after Vulcan, the Roman god of fire. Goodyear never grew rich from his discovery. His patent was widely ignored by competitors, he spent much of his life in court, and he died heavily in debt. In England, Thomas Hancock had reached similar results and obtained a British patent first.

D  Vulcanised rubber soon found uses everywhere, in hoses, belts, boots and the seals of steam engines. Demand rose steeply after 1888, when a Scottish vet named John Boyd Dunlop fitted his young son's tricycle with air-filled tyres, and again as the motor car spread across Europe and North America. At that time almost all the world's rubber came from wild trees in the Amazon basin, where the trees grew scattered through the forest, often many minutes' walk apart. Collecting the latex was slow and exhausting work, and the workers, many of whom were trapped by debt, were often treated brutally. The trade made the Brazilian city of Manaus fabulously wealthy, with an opera house and electric streetlights, but the wild trees could never produce enough to satisfy the growing demand.

E  The solution came from an unexpected direction. In 1876 Henry Wickham, an English adventurer, collected about seventy thousand seeds of the rubber tree in Brazil and shipped them to the Royal Botanic Gardens at Kew, near London. Only a small fraction germinated, but the seedlings were sent on to Ceylon and Malaya, where they thrived. Planters discovered that trees grown in neat rows were far easier to tap than wild ones, and by the 1910s the plantations of Southeast Asia were producing more rubber than the Amazon. The Brazilian boom collapsed almost overnight. Ironically, attempts to grow rubber on plantations in South America itself repeatedly failed. In 1928 an American car manufacturer cleared a huge area of forest for this purpose, but the trees, planted close together, were struck by a leaf blight that spread easily from one to the next. The disease had never reached Asia, and the trees there remained healthy.

F  The importance of the Asian plantations became obvious during the Second World War. When Japan occupied most of Southeast Asia in 1942, the Allies lost access to the great majority of their natural rubber almost at once. Without tyres, military vehicles and aircraft could not operate, and the United States launched an emergency programme to produce a synthetic substitute from petroleum. Dozens of factories were built within two years, the public was urged to hand in scrap rubber, and production of the man-made material rose from almost nothing to several hundred thousand tonnes a year. The war effort proved that rubber did not have to come from trees.

G  Today about two thirds of the world's rubber is synthetic, yet natural rubber remains irreplaceable for many purposes. It resists heat and tearing better than any man-made alternative, which is why it is still used for the tyres of lorries and aircraft. Almost all of it is grown in Southeast Asia, often on vast areas planted with a single kind of tree, and this worries scientists. If the leaf blight that destroyed the South American plantations ever crossed the oceans, the world's supply could be devastated. Researchers are therefore investigating other plants that could produce latex, including a desert shrub called guayule and a species of dandelion from central Asia, both of which can be grown in cooler or drier regions where the rubber tree would not survive.

passages.title: Sleep in Other Animals
paras: A  Sleep is one of the great puzzles of biology. For any animal, it is an extraordinarily risky habit. A sleeping creature cannot look for food, find a mate or watch for predators, and a long period of unconsciousness would seem to be a luxury that natural selection ought to have removed long ago. Yet it has not. Researchers have looked for an animal that does without sleep entirely, and so far they have failed to find one. Even creatures with no brain at all seem to need it. In 2017 a team of scientists observed that a species of jellyfish, which has no central nervous system, became less responsive and pulsed more slowly for several hours each night, and that it behaved sluggishly if it was disturbed during that time. Sleep, it seems, does not depend on a brain.

B  Although every species seems to sleep, the amount differs enormously. The brown bat spends around nineteen hours a day asleep, while giraffes and elephants in the wild manage on as little as two to four hours. Body size alone does not explain the difference. A more convincing explanation is that sleep reflects the dangers and demands of an animal's way of life. Grazing animals have to spend most of the day eating large quantities of low-quality food, and they are exposed to predators when they lie down, so they cannot afford long periods of rest. Bats, on the other hand, sleep hanging in safe, hidden roosts, and their sleep is tied to a high-energy lifestyle in which they hunt for only a few hours at dusk. When the risks are low and the food is plentiful, an animal can sleep more.

C  Some animals have evolved ways of sleeping and staying alert at the same time. Dolphins and some other whales sleep with only one half of the brain at a time, while the other half remains awake and controls breathing, because a dolphin that fell fully asleep could drown. Mothers and newborn calves go for weeks with almost no rest at all, a feat that would destroy a human being. Birds can do something similar. In an experiment with mallard ducks sleeping in a row, researchers found that the birds at the ends of the line kept one eye open for much longer than those in the middle. The eye was always the one facing outwards, and the half of the brain connected to it stayed awake. When the ducks changed places, their behaviour changed accordingly, which suggests that the animals were adjusting their alertness to the level of risk.

D  Even more remarkable is the discovery that some animals can sleep while they are on the move. Frigatebirds are seabirds that spend weeks over the ocean without landing, and scientists who fitted birds with small recorders were surprised to find that they slept in flight, in very short bursts, adding up to only about forty minutes a day, far less than they do on land. They seemed to rest one half of the brain at a time while gliding on rising air. Elephant seals, which spend months at sea hunting at great depths, were found to sleep during dives. When a seal falls asleep it rolls over and drifts downwards in a slow spiral, like a falling leaf, and the animal wakes up before it hits the bottom. Over a day, these naps add up to a total of only a couple of hours, yet the animals seem to remain healthy.

E  Such findings raise an obvious question about why sleep exists at all. Several theories compete. One holds that sleep is a way of saving energy, since a resting body burns fewer calories. Another argues that it is a time when memories are sorted and strengthened. Experiments on fruit flies support this idea: flies that were deprived of sleep were much poorer at learning and remembering than those that were allowed to rest. A third theory suggests that during sleep the brain clears away the waste products that build up when nerve cells are active during the day. None of these explanations has been proved, and they may all be partly correct. What is clear is that the animals that have been studied could not simply drop sleep without serious consequences. If they were prevented from sleeping for long enough, they became ill and eventually died.

F  Scientists hope that understanding sleep in other animals will help us to understand our own. Human sleep is notoriously fragile, and many people in modern societies sleep poorly, with consequences for health and safety. Animals that sleep in short bursts, or in only half of the brain, show that the process is far more flexible than anyone had assumed, and that it can be reshaped by the demands of the environment. This may offer clues about how to treat sleep disorders, or how to help people who must work at night. But researchers urge caution. Every species has adapted to its own circumstances, and what works for a frigatebird may well be useless for a person. The challenge now is to work out which of the features of sleep are universal and which are specific to a species.

passages.title: Is Multitasking a Myth?
paras: A  Job advertisements still ask for 'the ability to multitask', and applicants still list it proudly on their CVs. I believe this boast is largely empty, and that the word itself does a great deal of harm. It was borrowed in the 1960s from computing, where it described a machine with a single processor that appeared to run several programs at once by switching between them extremely quickly. Applying the same word to people gives the false impression that we, too, can handle several streams of work at the same time. We cannot. What we can do is switch rapidly from one task to another, and the evidence suggests that this is far more costly than most of us realise.

B  Consider a typical laboratory experiment. A team at a university asked volunteers to sort shapes and solve simple sums, either one task at a time or alternating between the two. When people alternated, they made more errors, and the total time they needed rose by as much as forty per cent. Crucially, the penalty grew as the tasks became more demanding. Switching between two easy chores cost little, while switching between two complex ones was ruinous. Psychologists explain this by what they call attention residue: when we move to a new task, part of our mind stays with the old one, and it takes time to let go. The more engrossing the first task, the more of our attention it keeps.

C  Defenders of multitasking point out, reasonably, that people do sometimes do two things at once. We walk and talk, or fold laundry while listening to the radio. But such activities are either largely automatic, or they draw on different mental resources, and neither case resembles the work that most employers have in mind. A more interesting objection concerns the small group of people nicknamed 'supertaskers'. In driving simulator tests, about two and a half per cent of participants were able to drive and hold a conversation with no measurable decline in either activity. I accept that they exist, and they are fascinating. However, they are so rare that they tell us nothing about how the other ninety-seven per cent should organise their working day. Designing an office around them would be like designing a school around the best sprinters.

D  What is more troubling is that those who multitask most seem to be the least aware of its effects. In one widely discussed survey, people who often used several media at once rated themselves as better than average at doing so, yet they performed worse than their colleagues on tests of ignoring distractions. It is possible, of course, that distractible people are simply more drawn to multitasking, rather than being damaged by it, and the research cannot settle the question. Either way, the confidence is misplaced. People who believe they are skilled have little reason to change how they work, and that is exactly why the myth persists.

E  The price is paid mainly in offices. The average worker is interrupted by a message, call or notification every few minutes, and one frequently quoted study estimated that it takes about twenty minutes to return fully to a task after a serious interruption. Some managers respond by sending staff on courses to help them cope with the flood of requests. I think this is the wrong approach. It treats the interruptions as inevitable and asks employees to adapt to them, when it would be more sensible to reduce the interruptions themselves. A handful of companies have introduced 'quiet hours', during which email is paused and meetings are banned, and several report that staff finish important work faster and with less stress. Such schemes cost almost nothing, and I would like to see them become the rule rather than the exception.

F  Some argue that the young, having grown up surrounded by screens, have developed a different mental make-up that allows them to juggle tasks more easily. I am unconvinced. Human brains change slowly, and a few decades of smartphones are unlikely to have rewired them. The limited evidence we have does not support the idea. In several tests, students who habitually switch between devices did no better than their peers, and sometimes did worse. It may be that young people are simply more comfortable with constant interruption, which is not the same as being good at it.

G  None of this means that we must abandon modern technology, or that it is wrong ever to do two things at once. It does mean that attention should be treated as a limited resource, like money or time, to be spent with care. Organisations that understand this will protect their staff from needless interruption, and individuals who understand it will think twice before opening another window. The more honest word for what most of us do all day is not multitasking at all. It is switching, and it is time we stopped pretending otherwise.
